title: Homogeneous degree-zero localization commutes with scalar extension
statement: Let $R,S$ be commutative rings with a ring homomorphism $R\to S$. Let $A=\bigoplus_{n\geq0}A_n$ be a nonnegatively graded commutative ring with a ring map $R\to A_0$. Put $C=S\otimes_R A$, with multiplication $(s\otimes a)(t\otimes b)=st\otimes ab$ and grading $C_n=S\otimes_R A_n$. For any homogeneous $f\in A_d$, $d>0$, put $f_S=1\otimes f$. Degree-zero homogeneous localization has the fraction notation of [def-nagata-homogeneous-localization-degree-zero]. The formula $$\lambda_f:S\otimes_R A_{(f),0}\longrightarrow C_{(f_S),0},\qquad s\otimes(a/f^m)\longmapsto (s\otimes a)/f_S^m\quad(a\in A_{md})$$ defines an isomorphism of $S$-algebras. No flatness assumption on $S$ over $R$ and no regularity assumption on $f$ is required.

proof.text: Put $H=A_{(f),0}$ and $K=C_{(f_S),0}$. The fraction relation in [def-nagata-homogeneous-localization-degree-zero] says $a/f^m=b/f^n$ iff $f^k(f^n a-f^m b)=0$ for some $k\geq0$. Equivalently, for some $L\geq m,n$ we have $f^{L-m}a=f^{L-n}b$ in $A_{Ld}$: for the forward direction take $L=m+n+k$, and for the reverse direction multiply this equality by $f^{m+n}$ to obtain a localization relation. Thus fractions can be compared at a common later denominator without cancelling $f$. In $C$, the relation $c/f_S^m=c\prime/f_S^n$ means $f_S^k(f_S^n c-f_S^m c\prime)=0$ for some $k\geq0$; taking $L=m+n+k$ gives $f_S^{L-m}c=f_S^{L-n}c\prime$. Conversely that equality multiplied by $f_S^{m+n}$ gives $f_S^L(f_S^n c-f_S^m c\prime)=0$.

proof.text: The graded piece identification in the statement needs no flatness: the degree-$j$ inclusion $i_j:A_j\to A$ and projection $p_j:A\to A_j$ are $R$-linear and satisfy $p_j i_j=1$. The maps on tensors, $s\otimes a\mapsto s\otimes i_j(a)$ and $s\otimes a\mapsto s\otimes p_j(a)$, respect balanced relations and still have composite $1$. Thus $S\otimes_R A_j$ identifies with its image $C_j$ in $C$, and every element of $C_j$ is a finite sum of tensors with numerator in $A_j$. For each $m$, the $R$-linear map $u_m:A_{md}\to H$, $a\mapsto a/f^m$, gives by the balanced tensor-product definition an $S$-linear map $q_m:C_{md}=S\otimes_R A_{md}\to S\otimes_R H$, with $q_m(\sum_i s_i\otimes a_i)=\sum_i s_i\otimes(a_i/f^m)$. This formula respects tensor relations because $u_m$ is additive and $R$-linear. Moreover $q_{m+1}(f_S c)=q_m(c)$: on a pure tensor this is $s\otimes(fa/f^{m+1})=s\otimes(a/f^m)$, and pure tensors generate. Iterating gives $q_L(f_S^{L-m}c)=q_m(c)$. If $c/f_S^m=c'/f_S^n$, step 1 gives equality of their numerators after passing to some $L$; applying $q_L$ proves $q_m(c)=q_n(c')$. Hence $\mu:K\to S\otimes_R H$, $c/f_S^m\mapsto q_m(c)$, is well defined. Addition is computed by putting both fractions over $f_S^L$ and using additivity of $q_L$, so $\mu$ is $S$-linear.

proof.text: For $s\in S$ and $a/f^m\in H$ set $b(s,a/f^m)=(s\otimes a)/f_S^m$. Equality of fractions in $H$ passes to equality in $K$ by the common-denominator equality in step 1. Putting two fractions over a common denominator proves additivity in the second variable; additivity in the first variable is the tensor relation, and $b(sr,a/f^m)=b(s,ra/f^m)$ for $r\in R$. Thus $b$ is balanced and induces the $S$-linear map $\lambda:S\otimes_R H\to K$ with the asserted formula. On pure tensors $\mu\lambda(s\otimes(a/f^m))=s\otimes(a/f^m)$, so this composite is the identity. For any $c/f_S^m$, write $c=\sum_i s_i\otimes a_i$ in $C_{md}$. Then $\lambda\mu(c/f_S^m)=\sum_i(s_i\otimes a_i)/f_S^m=c/f_S^m$, so the other composite is the identity.

source.place: Tag 01N2 (lemma-base-change-map-proj), omitted standard-open calculation; fraction convention of Tag 01M4 (lemma-standard-open)

proof.text: For $a\in A_{md}$ and $a'\in A_{nd}$, multiplication in the source tensor algebra and in the fraction ring gives $\lambda((s\otimes(a/f^m))(t\otimes(a'/f^n)))=(st\otimes aa')/f_S^{m+n}=\lambda(s\otimes(a/f^m))\lambda(t\otimes(a'/f^n))$. Distributing over finite sums proves multiplicativity on all elements. The unit $1\otimes(1/1)$ maps to $1/1$, and $s\otimes(1/1)$ maps to the coefficient $s$ in $K$. Thus $\lambda$ is an $S$-algebra homomorphism; step 3 makes it bijective, hence an $S$-algebra isomorphism. Every use of equality was by a power-annihilated relation rather than cancellation, so zero-divisors and arbitrary $R\to S$ are allowed.
